title: Question 2
stem:
A ball is thrown from a point P with an initial velocity $u$ of $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $50^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, as illustrated in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

The ball reaches maximum height at Q.

Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Picture $u$ as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. For the horizontal side, think whether it is adjacent to the $50^{\circ}$ angle at the ground.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Resolve Along the Horizontal**
You can treat the launch velocity as a vector that splits into two independent parts, horizontal and vertical. The horizontal part is the side adjacent to the $50^{\circ}$ angle, so it uses cosine.

Step 2: **Calculate the Value**
$$u_x = u \cos\theta = 12 \cos 50^{\circ} = 7.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
This stays constant all the way to Q because there is no horizontal acceleration when air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Now look for the vertical side of the same velocity triangle. Think whether this side is opposite the $50^{\circ}$ angle and what ratio that suggests.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Resolve Along the Vertical**
The vertical part is the side opposite the $50^{\circ}$ angle, so it uses sine. This is the part that will be changed by gravity.

Step 2: **Calculate the Value**
$$u_y = u \sin\theta = 12 \sin 50^{\circ} = 9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Keep this value for the next parts, it controls the time to the top and the maximum height.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Show that the maximum height reached by the ball is $4.3\ \text{m}$.

markscheme_points.text: alternative methods using time to maximum height of 0.94 s: $s = ut + \text{½}at^2$ and $t = 0.94$ (s)

hints: Hint 1: Focus only on vertical motion from P to Q. What must the vertical velocity be instantaneously at the highest point Q?
Hint 2: Link that starting vertical speed of $9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, the final speed at Q, acceleration $-g$, and height $h$ with a SUVAT equation that does not need time.
parts.proper_answer: At Q, $v_y = 0$. Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ vertically: $0 = 9.2^2 - 2 \times 9.81 \times h$, giving $h = 4.3 \text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the Condition at the Top**
Going up, gravity slows the vertical motion at $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards. At the very top Q the ball momentarily stops moving up before it starts coming down, so vertical velocity $v_y = 0$.

Step 2: **Apply SUVAT Vertically**
Take upwards as positive, so $u = +9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, $a = -9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and displacement is height $h$:
$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$
$$0 = 9.2^2 + 2(-9.81)h$$

Step 3: **Show the Height**
$$h = \frac{9.2^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 4.3 \text{ m}$$
This matches the required value, confirming the calculation.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Determine the magnitude of the displacement $PQ$.
hints: Hint 1: PQ is the straight line from launch to the top, not the curved path. You already know its vertical side is $4.3 \text{ m}$, so you need to find its horizontal side first.
Hint 2: Find the time to reach Q by thinking how long gravity at $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ takes to reduce the $9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ upward speed to zero.
Hint 3: During that same time the horizontal motion has no acceleration, so horizontal distance is simply constant horizontal speed multiplied by time.
Hint 4: Combine the perpendicular horizontal and vertical displacements to get the straight-line magnitude.
parts.proper_answer: Time to Q $t = 0.94 \text{ s}$, horizontal distance $x = 7.2 \text{ m}$, displacement $PQ = \sqrt{4.3^2 + 7.2^2} = 8.4 \text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Time to Reach Q**
Vertically, velocity falls from $9.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to zero under $g$. Using $v = u + at$ upwards:
$$0 = 9.2 - 9.81t$$
$$t = \frac{9.2}{9.81} = 0.94 \text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Find the Horizontal Distance to Q**
Horizontally there is no acceleration, so the $7.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ speed is constant for this whole time:
$$x = u_x t = 7.7 \times 0.938 = 7.2 \text{ m}$$
This is the base of the right-angled triangle P to Q.

Step 3: **Combine to Get Straight-Line Displacement**
PQ is the hypotenuse with vertical side $h = 4.3 \text{ m}$ and horizontal side $x = 7.2 \text{ m}$. By Pythagoras:
$$PQ = \sqrt{x^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{7.23^2 + 4.3^2}$$
$$PQ = 8.4 \text{ m}$$
